with_skill.answer:
A grain overlay is a **component**, so it is merged into your composition. It is not included as a separate file the way a block is.

**Installed component (default path):** `compositions/components/grain-overlay.html`

**Integrating into an existing composition:**

1. Open the installed file and read it.
2. Copy its HTML elements into your composition's `<div data-composition-id="...">`.
3. Copy its `<style>` block into your composition's styles.
4. If it has a `<script>`, copy the contents into your composition's script, before your timeline code.
5. If the snippet's comment block describes GSAP timeline integration, add those calls to your timeline.

The component has no dimensions or duration of its own. It takes on the host composition's canvas and timing.

**Standalone block, for comparison:**

A block is a self-contained sub-composition with its own dimensions, duration, and timeline. You don't paste its markup into your host. You reference the file from the host's `index.html` with a `data-composition-src` element that carries these attributes:

- `data-composition-src`: path to the block HTML file
- `data-composition-id`: must match the block's internal ID
- `data-start`: when it appears in the host timeline, in seconds
- `data-duration`: how long it plays
- `data-width` / `data-height`: its canvas size
- `data-track-index`: a Studio timeline row only; use CSS `z-index` for layering

**Key differences:**

| | Component (grain overlay) | Block |
|---|---|---|
| Default location | `compositions/components/` | `compositions/` |
| How it's used | Markup, CSS, and JS are pasted into the host | Referenced with `data-composition-src` |
| Own size/duration | No | Yes |
| Timing | Inherits the host's | Set with `data-start` and `data-duration` |
| Layering | Standard CSS in the host | `z-index`, not `data-track-index` |

The grain overlay is the right fit for a texture over the whole composition. A block would be the right fit for a self-contained segment with its own timing.

baseline.answer:
I can't see the grain overlay's code or your composition, so this is a general comparison, not advice tied to your files.

**Integrating into an existing composition**

- The overlay sits inside a parent container, so it inherits that container's size, position, and clipping. The parent usually needs `position: relative` (or the equivalent) so an absolutely positioned overlay covers the right area.
- You control stacking through the parent's layers. The grain can sit above the content for a film-like texture, or below a semi-transparent background.
- It can share the parent's data and state, so it can react to things like theme or hover without extra wiring.
- It adds no extra wrapper or page-level element, which keeps the layout simpler.
- It's tied to that section. Moving or reusing the section means moving the overlay too, and it may pick up unintended styles from the parent.

**Standalone block**

- It's self-contained with its own sizing and positioning, so it behaves the same wherever it's placed.
- It's easier to reuse across pages or sections and to test in isolation.
- It usually needs a wrapper or explicit positioning to cover a target area, and it can compete with other layers for stacking order.
- It may add an extra DOM node or layout element.

**Practical checks either way**

- Make sure the overlay doesn't block clicks (`pointer-events: none`).
- Confirm the z-index and any `mix-blend-mode` produce the intended result over the content.
- Check that `overflow: hidden` on the parent isn't clipping the grain at the edges.
- If the grain animates, consider reduced-motion settings.

**Recommendation:** If the grain is meant for one section and should respond to that section's content or theme, integrate it into the composition. If you want the same texture across several unrelated areas, use the standalone block. The only fact I have is that the grain overlay is installed as a component snippet. I can't see its code or the surrounding composition, so this comparison is general. Check the snippet's actual markup and styles before relying on any of it.

**Integrating a snippet into an existing composition**

- **Placement:** The overlay goes inside a container you already have. Its position depends on the parent's layout, so you may need to place it carefully in the tree.
- **Positioning context:** An absolutely positioned grain layer usually needs a positioned ancestor (`position: relative`) to cover the right area. Without one, it can cover the whole page or land in the wrong place.
- **Stacking:** Grain is typically layered above content with `pointer-events: none` and a z-index. Existing z-index values, transforms, or `overflow: hidden` in the parent can clip it or put it beneath other elements.
- **Inherited styles:** Fonts, colors, blend modes, and CSS variables from the parent can affect the overlay. Scoped class names can also collide with existing ones.
- **Benefit:** It matches the surrounding design and reuses the parent's sizing, theme, and responsive behavior.
- **Cost:** It is harder to move or reuse, and changes to the parent can break it.

**Using it as a standalone block**

- **Self-contained:** It carries its own wrapper, dimensions, and positioning, so it works wherever it's dropped in.
- **Predictable:** It doesn't depend on the parent's layout, stacking, or styles, which makes it easier to test in isolation.
- **Reusable:** You can place it on different pages or in different compositions without rework.
- **Cost:** It may duplicate styles or wrappers, may cover more of the page than intended, and may need explicit sizing to fit the design.

**Choosing between them**

- Use the snippet inside a composition when the grain should be scoped to one section, sit within a specific layout, or share that section's theme.
- Use a standalone block when the grain is a page-wide texture or you need it in several unrelated places.

The only fact I have is that a grain overlay is installed as a component snippet. I don't have its code, props, or markup, so this is general guidance. Check it against the snippet's actual API.

**Integrating into an existing composition**
- Place the snippet as a child of the element it should cover, or as a sibling later in the stacking order, so it layers above the content it textures.
- It typically needs to be absolutely positioned to fill its parent, with `pointer-events: none` so it doesn't block clicks.
- It inherits the parent's size, theme variables, and stacking context. The grain follows the composition's bounds and responds to its styling.

**Standalone block**
- It is self-contained, with its own dimensions, placement, and any styling it needs.
- It can be dropped anywhere and reused across compositions without changing their structure.
- You must size and position it explicitly, and it won't pick up the surrounding theme unless you pass values in.
- It adds a separate element to the layout, which can affect spacing or flow if it isn't taken out of flow.

**Choosing between them**
- Use the snippet when the grain should apply to one specific composition and follow its bounds.
- Use the standalone block when the grain is a reusable visual element or must sit outside an existing layout.
